title: Samaria or Imbros? Choosing Between Crete's Two Best-Known Gorges
seoTitle: Samaria vs Imbros Gorge: Which Crete Hike to Choose
seoDescription: Samaria is 16 km and 5-7 hours of walking; Imbros is 8 km and 2-3 hours. Length, descent, season, crowds, cost and transport compared, with who each suits.
summary: Choose Samaria if you want the landmark and can commit a full twelve-hour day to 16 kilometres of continuous descent from 1,250 metres to the sea, ending at a village reachable only by boat. Choose Imbros if you want the same limestone-corridor scenery in 8 kilometres and 2 to 3 hours of easy downhill walking, with a vehicle waiting at the end, no ferry timetable to catch, and the option of going in any month of the year. Samaria is open only from 1 May to 31 October and is the busiest hiking route in Greece; Imbros runs year-round and carries a fraction of the traffic. For most visitors - families, anyone with knees, anyone who only has half a day - Imbros is the better hike. Samaria is worth it if the length is the point.
body:
This is the decision almost every visitor to western Crete ends up making, and it is usually framed wrongly - as though Imbros were a consolation prize. It is not. They are different walks with different costs, and the right answer depends on how much of your holiday you are willing to spend walking downhill.

## Side by side

| | Samaria | Imbros |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Length** | 16 km | 8 km |
| **Start altitude** | Xyloskalo, Omalos Plateau, ~1,250 m | Imbros village, ~780 m |
| **Total descent** | ~1,250 m, to sea level | ~600 m, to Komitades |
| **Walking time** | 5-7 hours | 2-3 hours |
| **Full day, door to door** | About 12 hours; pickup 06:30 | 5-7 hours; pickup 07:00 |
| **Difficulty** | Demanding - length plus sustained downhill pressure on the knees | Easy - well-defined path, no scrambling |
| **Season** | 1 May to 31 October only | All year, daily |
| **Crowds** | The busiest hiking route in Greece; coach groups from first light in July and August | A fraction of Samaria's traffic |
| **Ends at** | Agia Roumeli, on the Libyan Sea - no road access | Komitades, on the road network |
| **Getting back** | Ferry to Chora Sfakion, then road; the ferry timetable governs the day | The van meets you at the exit |
| **Third-party costs** | 10 EUR entrance, 17 EUR ferry per adult (8.50 EUR child 5-12), optional 2 EUR shuttle bus | Entrance fee paid at the gate |
| **Signature sight** | Sideroportes, the Iron Gates - a few metres wide beneath vertical cliffs | Stenada Imbrou - walls under two metres apart, tall shaded corridors |
| **Suits** | Fit walkers who want the landmark and have a whole day | Families, casual walkers, bad knees, short schedules, off-season trips |

## What the walks actually feel like

### Samaria

The day starts before dawn because it has to. From Xyloskalo, on the edge of the Omalos Plateau at about 1,250 metres, the first section is steep stone steps cut into the mountainside - the hardest part of the route, and the part your knees remember. The gorge then opens out through cypress and pine, past the abandoned village of Samaria at roughly the midpoint, before dropping into the lower riverbed where the walls close in. At Sideroportes the gorge narrows to a few metres with cliffs going up several hundred metres almost vertically.

After that it flattens, warms and thins out. The last stretch to Agia Roumeli is hot, exposed and unglamorous - and it is where most people find out how tired they are. Then there is a swim, a taverna, and a ferry.

It is a genuinely great walk. It is also a twelve-hour day of which five to seven hours are spent going downhill on stone.

### Imbros

Imbros starts at about 780 metres at the edge of Imbros village and follows the dry riverbed south. The upper section is open, then the limestone walls rise and the canyon narrows. At Stenada Imbrou the walls come to less than two metres apart and run vertically overhead - shaded corridors of rock that are, on a smaller scale, the same experience as the Iron Gates.

Below the narrows the gorge widens again and the walking gets easier still. It ends at Komitades, a village on the road, a few minutes from Chora Sfakion and the south coast.

The gorge also carries real history: in 1941 it was the route Allied troops used to withdraw over the White Mountains to the south coast for evacuation.

## Cost, honestly

Samaria's headline price looks better in a group and worse in a pair, because the guided day is a flat group rate plus per-person entrance and ferry tickets. Imbros is a sliding per-person price. Using the published rates:

| Group size | Samaria, all-in per person | Imbros, per person |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 202 EUR | 145 EUR |
| 4 | 114.50 EUR | 72.50 EUR |
| 6 | 85.33 EUR | 58 EUR |
| 8 | 70.75 EUR | 44 EUR |

The Samaria figures are the 350 EUR group price divided by the group, plus 10 EUR entrance and 17 EUR adult ferry per person; the optional 2 EUR shuttle bus at the gorge exit is extra. The Imbros figures exclude the gorge entrance fee, which is paid at the gate and is not published in advance. Imbros also includes a professional photoshoot at no extra cost.

## Transport logistics - the part people underestimate

This is the real difference between the two.

**Samaria is one-way and ends where there is no road.** Agia Roumeli can only be left on foot or by boat. That means the ferry to Chora Sfakion, then a vehicle back over the mountains. The consequence is that the ferry timetable, not your walking pace, sets the schedule: if the group is slow, the whole day breaks. It is also why a guided day exists at all - the driver meets you on the far side of a mountain range, several hours from where you started.

**Imbros ends on the road.** Komitades is a village with a road through it. The van that dropped you at the top meets you at the bottom. There is no boat, no timetable and no consequence to walking slowly.

## Season

Samaria is normally open from **1 May to 31 October** and closed for the rest of the year, because winter and spring flooding makes the riverbed dangerous. If you are in Crete in November, March or April, the decision has been made for you.

Imbros runs **all year**. It can close briefly after heavy rain, but in practice it is the winter and shoulder-season gorge.

## Crowds

Samaria is the most walked trail in Greece. In July and August, coaches start unloading at Xyloskalo before sunrise, and the narrow sections - including the Iron Gates - queue. Starting early is not an advantage there; everyone starts early.

Imbros carries far fewer people, and because it is short, walkers spread out quickly. If solitude matters to you, this is not a close call.

## So which one?

**Walk Samaria if:** you are a confident walker, you want the landmark specifically, you can lose an entire day to it, your knees are sound, and you are in Crete between May and October.

**Walk Imbros if:** you have children, you have half a day rather than a whole one, you have knee or heart problems, you would rather photograph a gorge than survive one, you are visiting outside the summer season, or you want to be back at the coast in time to swim.

**Consider both if** you are here for a week. They are two hours apart by road, they are not the same walk, and doing Imbros first tells you honestly whether you want Samaria.

### A third option worth knowing about

You can also walk Samaria from the bottom. Take the ferry to Agia Roumeli, walk up the gorge to the Iron Gates and back - about 6 kilometres return, uphill on the way out and downhill on the way back, on the least crowded part of the trail. You see the most dramatic section without committing to 16 kilometres. It is not offered as a standard tour, but it is the sensible compromise for anyone who wants the Iron Gates and not the day.

faqs.q: Is Imbros Gorge easier than Samaria?
faqs.a: Considerably. Imbros is 8 km with about 600 metres of descent and takes 2 to 3 hours on a well-defined path. Samaria is 16 km with about 1,250 metres of descent and takes 5 to 7 hours, with a steep, stepped opening section that is hard on the knees. Imbros is the family option; Samaria is not.

faqs.q: Which gorge is better in Crete, Samaria or Imbros?
faqs.a: Samaria is the more spectacular walk and the recognised landmark, with the Iron Gates as its centrepiece. Imbros gives you the same kind of narrow limestone corridor scenery at Stenada Imbrou in a quarter of the effort, with no ferry to catch and no seasonal closure. For most visitors Imbros is the better use of a day; for walkers who want the full traverse, Samaria is worth the twelve hours.

faqs.q: Can I hike Samaria Gorge with children?
faqs.a: It is not recommended. Sixteen kilometres of continuous descent over stone is a lot for a child, and there is no way to stop halfway - once you are in the gorge, the only exits are the top and the bottom. Imbros, at 8 km with an easy path and a vehicle at the end, is the gorge to take children into.

faqs.q: Do I have to take a ferry after Samaria Gorge?
faqs.a: Yes. The gorge ends at Agia Roumeli, which has no road access, so the only way out is the ferry to Chora Sfakion (17 EUR per adult, 8.50 EUR per child aged 5-12) and then a vehicle back over the mountains. The ferry timetable sets the pace of the whole day. Imbros has no such constraint - it ends at Komitades, on the road.

faqs.q: When is Samaria Gorge open, and what do I do outside those months?
faqs.a: Samaria normally opens on 1 May and closes on 31 October. Outside that window, Imbros is the answer: it runs year-round, the path holds up in cooler weather, and the winter light in the narrows is arguably better than the summer version.

faqs.q: How much does each gorge hike cost?
faqs.a: The guided Samaria day is 350 EUR flat for up to eight people, plus 10 EUR entrance and 17 EUR ferry per adult - so roughly 202 EUR per person for two, or 70.75 EUR per person for eight. Imbros is priced per person on a sliding scale: 145 EUR each for two, down to 44 EUR each for eight, plus the entrance fee paid at the gate. Imbros also includes a photoshoot.

faqs.q: Can I do both gorges in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a reasonable plan for a week-long stay. They are about two hours apart by road and are genuinely different walks. Doing Imbros first is a useful test: if 8 km downhill left you comfortable, Samaria is realistic; if it did not, you have saved yourself a difficult day.
